stories.title: Trump signs executive order waiving new Russia sanctions
stories.summary: US President Donald ⁠Trump has waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs - days before they were to take effect under a law he signed last month, including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas. In an executive order released by the White House yesterday, Mr Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States. The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Mr Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticising Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader. Weeks before US midterm elections in which Mr Trump's Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely attributed ‌to the US-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have ⁠said. The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions. The order said the waiver will remain ‌in effect until Mr Trump or his top officials determine that "further action is appropriate".

stories.title: Connolly says human rights must guide response to crises
stories.summary: President Catherine Connolly has told a meeting with 11 other European presidents that "human dignity, equality, and human rights" must guide how the European Union responds to crises like climate change and war. President Connolly has attended her first ‘Arraiolos Group’ meeting of non-executive Heads of State from across Europe at the Brdo Estate outside Ljubljana, Slovenia. During her speech, President Connolly posed a number of questions to her counterparts. "Can we credibly talk about peace, progress and security while at the same time tolerating the normalisation of war and genocide?" she asked. "Can we address the existential threat posed by climate change, deepening inequality and the increasing number of people living in poverty, while simultaneously believing that we can continue with business as usual? "Can we expect or deserve to retain credibility when our responses to these challenges, and to the abuse of power, are manifestly inconsistent?"

stories.title: Uisce Éireann CEO defends €118,000 pay rise
stories.summary: Uisce Éireann CEO Niall Gleeson has defended a €118,000 increase in his overall salary to €391,953 - saying he and the utility are providing value for money to the public. Mr Gleeson was asked about the pay rise during the latest meeting of the Dáil Public Accounts Committee, amid separate questions over a €4,000 spend on PR advice before attending the meeting with TDs and senators. During a robust exchange, Sinn Féin TD Cathy Bennett told Mr Gleeson, "I have to say you must be doing an amazing job" because his salary has increased by €118,000, a rise first reported in July. Ms Bennett compared the rise to the far smaller increase being sought by public sector workers taking part in nationwide strikes, before asking: "How does someone receive that increase in one year?" The Sinn Féin TD said, "I don't know how you can sit here and condone it [the salary]", referencing problems some of her constituents in Co Monaghan have in terms of accessing clean water, water connections, and water that is not "brown". In response, Mr Gleeson said his pay rise was agreed after "an independent review of all salaries" at utilities, and that "the board [of Uisce Éireann] took the recommendations" and agreed to them.

stories.title: AIB cuts 4-year fixed rate for mortgages over €250,000
stories.summary: AIB has today announced a cut of up to 0.35% on its four-year fixed rate for mortgages over €250,000. AIB said the new rate, which is available immediately for new and existing customers, will benefit those whose homes do not have a Building Energy Rating of B3 or higher. The bank said that customers are increasingly opting for the certainty of a competitively priced fixed rate after the ECB increased rates by 0.25% twice this year. Almost nine in ten new AIB customers have opted for a fixed rate this year, it noted. AIB said a monthly repayment on its new €350,000 AIB High Value 4-year fixed rate mortgage, with a loan to value of 50 to 80% over a 25-year term, will be €1,695.30. The previous monthly repayment would have been €1,750.82, representing a saving of €55.52 a month, €666.24 a year, or €4,715.72 over the 25-year term of the mortgage.

stories.title: Pope holds phone call with Putin during hospital recovery
stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV has held a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, the Vatican said, as the pope continues to recover in hospital after undergoing surgery for lung cancer. The Vatican said the pope is showing "steady improvement" following Tuesday's surgery. During the call with Mr Putin, the American pontiff expressed "deep concern" for the humanitarian situation in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky. Pope Leo urged Mr Putin for a truce to allow the entry of first aid and food supplies into the town, the Vatican said, and to permit a voluntary evacuation of the civilian population. The call with Mr Putin came after the Vatican said that the pope is now able to do normal daily activities with full autonomy. The pope will make his first public appearance since his hospitalisation on Sunday to deliver the traditional Angelus prayer, while preparations continue for his planned November trip to South America, the Vatican said.

stories.summary: Before the recent international break, the SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division title race had coalesced into a mouth-watering three-team battle. But after Monday's Dublin derby between Shamrock Rovers and Bohemians, it feels like the latter are all but mathematically out of the reckoning. Bohs find themselves six points adrift of the reigning champions with just nine points to play for. All of which has swung the onus towards St Patrick's Athletic in terms of who can prevent Shamrock Rovers winning a sixth title in seven years. Stephen Kenny's side have a game in hand on the Hoops. But they have had to wait in the wings since they last played almost a month ago in a nervy 1-0 away win at now relegated Sligo Rovers on 19 September. All of a sudden, the Saints now face a decisive long weekend starting with Shelbourne's visit to Richmond Park tonight, followed by an away assignment at an improving Derry City on Monday.

stories.title: Cullen excited by 'good little tweak' to bonus-points
stories.summary: Since its introduction in 2020, the revamped pool stage of the Investec Champions Cup is yet to really catch on. Supporters have been yearning for the good old days; pools of four, everyone playing each other home and away, and a round of back-to-back ties just before Christmas. You could have set your watch to it. Those days aren't coming back any time soon - unless the various leagues can find a spare weekend to hand back to the EPCR - but tournament organiser have this year taken some steps to put extra excitement and a competitive edge into the pool stage sprint. One of these rules won't necessarily apply until the final round of games. Up until this season, the top four teams in each pool advance to the Round of 16, but this year's change means only the top three in each pool will be guaranteed knockout rugby, with the next four best teams in terms of overall record joining them. The logic behind it is to eliminate what has happened in previous seasons, where a team has qualified with just one win from four games, while a team with two wins in a different pool has missed out, such as last season, where Leicester Tigers and Bulls made it to through with just one pool win each, while the Sharks were eliminated with two. Crucially, it doesn't eliminate the possibility that a team could qualify with just one win, but it almost guarantees they cannot qualify at the expense of teams with more wins. Applying last season's criteria to last season the Sharks would have replaced Leicester Tigers in the knockout stage.

stories.title: Wexford Festival Opera - watch Rossini's L'equivoco stravagante
stories.summary: We proudly present a live presentation from this year's Wexford Festival Opera - L'equivoco stravagante by Gioachino Rossini, with a libretto by Gaetano Gasbarri. A joyous early work by Rossini, L'equivoco stravagante is a fast-paced, playful exploration of social climbing and the lengths we go to for love. Musically brilliant, it’s the ultimate fun night at the opera. A sparkling farce of absurd misunderstandings, youthful wit, rapid-fire ensemL'equivoco stravagantebles and comic excess, L’equivoco stravagante was Rossini’s first large-scale opera. It vanished from the repertoire after falling foul of the censor due to its subversive libretto. Wexford was one of the first companies to present it in 1968. The title means something like 'The Bizzare Misunderstanding' and premiered in Bologna in 1811, when the young composer was still only 19 years of age. This production returns following a historic public vote last summer. In a first for the Festival, audiences from 30 countries chose (by way of a vote) the 'fun’ opera for the 75th Anniversary, marking the first time a production has been selected by popular demand. Directed by Max Hoehn and conducted by Riccardo Bisatti, both making their Wexford debuts, this production is a masterclass in Rossini’s signature buffo (comic) style. In it we meet Gamberotto, a wealthy farmer with high-society ambitions for his bookish daughter, Ernestina. While he attempts to marry her off to the rich (but dim-witted) Buralicchio, the penniless Ermanno has other plans. What follows is a whirlwind of subversion, outrageous disguises, and a ‘bizarre misunderstanding’ involving a fake identity that once proved too scandalous for the 19th-century censors. stories.title: Bob Geldof reflects on Live Aid and Ireland's generosity
stories.summary: Singer, author and humanitarian Bob Geldof has said Live Aid offered a glimpse of the Ireland he had always believed existed, praising the generosity and kindness shown in response to the charity event. Live Aid took place on July 13, 1985, with simultaneous concerts at Wembley Stadium in London and John F Kennedy Stadium in Philadelphia. Organised by Geldof and musician Midge Ure, the event brought together music legends including Queen, U2, David Bowie, Elton John, Madonna and Paul McCartney to raise funds for famine relief in Ethiopia. Geldof was at Wembley Stadium as the concert was about to begin when the Irish production team contacted him. The women were waiting outside and wanted to hand them over. Concerned that they might later regret such a personal sacrifice, Geldof asked the organisers to ensure they were certain of their decision. He instructed them to hold the rings for a week, giving the women the opportunity to reclaim them if they changed their minds. Reflecting on Ireland's generosity, he said: "Pro rata, as we all know famously, this country did more than any other country in the world."

stories.title: How Ireland Fashion Week created a homecoming for Irish designers
stories.summary: Sarah Magliocco looks back on Ireland Fashion Week 2026, speaking to the organisers, designers and creatives behind a showcase that brought the world stage to Irish design. Ireland Fashion Week has just closed its second year, and with a stacked schedule, impressive venues, international interest and scores of social media impressions, it's secured all the hallmarks that befit fellow fashion weeks across the world. However, the distinctly Irish elements have not been lost in that process, and nowhere was that more apparent than the theme of this year’s events. 'Coming Home: An Island In Motion’ made reference to Ireland’s global impact on the fashion industry, while influencing designers to reflect on the idea of coming home, a concept held so dearly by a diaspora that stretches to all corners of the earth. "But that's changed in the last few years, in particular where people are able to come home but also people don't necessarily have to leave, and we also have people from the rest of the world coming to Ireland and calling it home." A Galway native, McDonnell relocated to Paris to pursue her career in the luxury fashion industry while still in university. She was called home to create a platform where Irish design could be appreciated by a wider audience and Irish creatives would have paid opportunities to showcase their work.

stories.title: Meetings on structure of public sector pay talks to begin
stories.summary: Meetings to agree a structure for public sector pay talks are expected to get under way this weekend. Yesterday trade unions agreed to suspend plans for a 24-hour strike on Wednesday after it was announced that an independent third party, Kevin Foley, is to conduct an exercise aimed at constructing a basis for formal negotiations at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC). Mr Foley, a former Chair of the Labour Court and current Chair of the WRC, will be assisted by one trade union representative, ICTU General Secretary Owen Reidy, and one Government representative, Oonagh Buckley, who is Secretary General of the Department of the Environment. They will meet with all sides in the dispute, starting this morning, and work towards constructing a framework for pay negotiations at the WRC. While Wednesday's strike has been suspended, industrial action in the form of a work-to-rule will continue across the public sector. More than 300,000 public sector workers including nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants, engaged in strike action last Wednesday over delays in agreeing a new public sector pay deal.

stories.title: Pensioner 'back counting pennies' as council doubles rent
stories.summary: Ann Dolan is in the sitting room of her house in Hazelwood in Bray. One of the biggest local authority estates in Wicklow, she has lived here for 50 years, rearing three children. Last month, she received a letter from the council. "I opened it … and I thought it has to be a mistake … I was just in shock, I really couldn't believe it was real," she said. The letter informed her that her rent was about to double – up from around €200 per month, to €400. "When I was younger, I went through this sort of thing, poverty, bringing three kids up, and then we're back doing it again," she said. She added: "You're at my age again. You're back counting the pennies, where you should be able to sit back and not have to worry about all this now."

stories.title: Aontú to table no confidence motion in Helen McEntee
stories.summary: Aontú is to table a Dáil motion of no confidence in the Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee over her handling of garda whistleblower allegations. Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín confirmed his party will use its Dáil time on 4 November to bring forward the motion which will focus on Ms McEntee's tenure as Minister for Justice between 2020 and 2025. The programme revealed that two people who handled protected disclosures made by garda whistleblowers have themselves blown the whistle, alleging that reforms introduced to protect those who speak out have been undermined by senior management. They were among four garda whistleblowers speaking publicly for the first time in the programme. The Dáil heard claims that Ms McEntee "usurped the role" of the Office of the Protected Disclosure Commission by referring to An Garda Síochana a protected disclosure made to her. The Fine Gael Meath East TD rejected the claims, insisting she adhered to the law "at all times".

stories.title: Diesel prices: can US-Russia deal ease global pressure?
stories.summary: Diesel prices have continued their upward trend during September and October, surpassing €2.10 per litre this month. According to the latest estimates from AA, the national average reached €2.14 in October, a 24% increase compared to February this year. The cost of fuel, which is crucial for logistics and farming, as well as for millions of private motorists, has soared globally. Diesel margins, or the "crack spread" - which measures how much money refineries make from selling a barrel of diesel compared with the price of crude oil - have also reached record levels. There is a cost in turning "something useless into something useful", Dr Paul Deane, Senior Lecturer at the University College Cork, explained. "That is essentially what we call crack spreads or refinery spreads. That reflects the amount of money that the refinery gets for converting oil into a useful product." Back in February, refineries earned around $32 per barrel of diesel. In September, this margin rose to $107.

stories.title: Settlers burn olive trees, injure journalist in West Bank
stories.summary: Clad in black and with their faces masked, dozens of militant Israeli settlers burned olive trees and threw rocks at Palestinians in a coordinated attack on a West Bank village's annual harvest that injured at least two people including a journalist. Some 80 settlers, some of them carrying gas canisters, descended from a hill above a terraced olive grove where villagers from Abu Falah had gathered to pick ripe fruit, a cherished annual tradition in Palestinian life, Reuters witnesses said. The settlers took positions in front of the terraced lanes of olive trees. Some of them used slings to launch rocks towards Palestinian villagers, who descended towards the bottom of the hill before picking up and throwing stones to defend themselves. "The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes," said Moutaz Abdelhadi, 42, a farmer who witnessed the attack in Abu Falah. Partway through the attack, at least two Israeli military jeeps sped through the area, kicking up dust as villagers ran out of their way.

stories.title: Bradley: Win two more games and we know what that brings
stories.summary: After losing away to Galway United Shamrock Rovers manager Stephen Bradley is demanding an improvement from his side ahead of their final two league games of the season, with a successful defence of the Premier Division title still in their own hands. First-half goals and some resolute defending saw the hosts record a deserved 2-0 victory at Eamonn Deacy Park. An outcome that could have been worse for the Hoops had St Patrick's Athletic, who have a game in hand, not relinquished their half-time advantage at home to Shelbourne. Bohemians' win over Waterford keeps them mathematically in the title race but Bradley's side are at home to relegated Sligo Rovers before rounding out their campaign at Dundalk. As for the game itself, Bradley was offering no excuses and dismissed talk of fatigue after Monday's hard-fought win against Bohemians. "When you give Galway the start that we gave them it will always be a difficult game. And when you give away the goals that we did it becomes more difficult. Galway were good tonight, got two goals and held on. No complaining in terms of fatigue, we're just to playing every few days at this club and we've done it for a long time. It is what it is and we don't lose the game because of that." Galway boss John Caulfield was pleased with the response his showed after last weekend's FAI Cup semi-final loss to Derry City. "From the start of the season we were tipped as the team to get relegated because we had so many changes, a brand new team. We got a cup semi-final and while it was disappointing last week, a lot of the crowd came back tonight because they knew Shamrock Rovers were in town. Pico (Lopes) and Graham Burke absolutely fantastic players and we knew tonight we had to be disciplined.

stories.title: Clifford disappointed over Fossa manager's departure
stories.summary: Paudie Clifford says it was "disappointing" that Fossa manager Jerome Stack departed suddenly as the club prepare for a Munster intermediate football campaign. Stack, who brought the club to successive Kerry intermediate finals, with last month’s victory over Kilcummin securing senior status for the club just outside Killarney for the first time in its history. However, five weeks out from a Munster semi-final against Tipperary or Limerick opposition, Fossa are on the hunt for a new manager. It has been reported that Stack felt aggrieved over the involvement of seven Fossa players - including Paudie and his brother David - in training for divisional side East Kerry rather than the club. East Kerry exited the championship last weekend at the quarter-final stage. Speaking at the launch of the AIB Club Championships 2026/27, Clifford paid tribute to the ground work done by Stack, admitting it wasn’t ideal preparation with a Munster campaign to plan for.

stories.title: O'Neill heartened by Celtic resolve despite Lisbon loss
stories.summary: Martin O'Neill hailed Celtic’s second-half display in the 4-1 Europa League defeat by Benfica which left them with no points from six in the league phase. Colombia striker Jhon Duran scored with a penalty after just five minutes in Lisbon after being fouled by Hoops defender Dane Murray and added a second in the 35th minute, after defender Alexander Bah had notched midway through the first half. Celtic reduced the deficit through Camilo Duran in the 63rd minute before Benfica substitute Vangelis Pavlidis fired in a fourth with two minutes remaining. Celtic lost 3-1 at home to Hungarian outfit Ferencvaros in their first Europa League game at Parkhead, but boss O’Neill insists he witnessed enough in the second half performance in Portugal to give him belief. He told TNT Sports: "We started quite well, we forced a corner early on, and just trying to get into the game, they got a goal. The last thing you want to do is concede so early on. "And then at 2-0 we’ve got a great, great chance to make it 2-1 and within a few minutes they make it 3-0.

stories.title: Edogbo signs new contract up to 2029
stories.summary: Munster and Ireland second-row Edwin Edogbo has signed a new two-year contract with the province and the IRFU that will see him remain in red until 2029. The 23-year-old made his Ireland debut back in February's Six Nations win over Italy, and has become a vital cog in Clayton McMillan's team since returning from successive long-term injuries across 2024 and early 2025. Having come through the ranks with Cobh Pirates, Edogbo was the first player from Cobh to enter the Munster academy back in 2021, and was soon followed by younger brother Seán. The lock made his Munster debut away to the Dragons in 2022, making eight appearances in their URC title winning season that same season. After missing all of the 2024/25 season through injury, Edogbo made his long-awaited return to the fold last year, making 16 appearances as well as his Champions Cup debut and later his Ireland debut. Speaking of the news, Munster head coach spoke of Edogbo's unique physical abilitiy.

stories.title: Cinema at the edge of Ireland - Disappear Here returns to Donegal
stories.summary: Set between the mountains and the Atlantic on Donegal's wild Inishowen Peninsula, Disappear Here is a film festival with a difference… Founder and Festival Director Michael McLaughlin tells more ahead of this year's installment, which runs from October 16th - 18th. When I started Disappear Here Film Festival in Ballyliffin in 2017, the idea was to bring films to the north-west that people here might never otherwise get the chance to see. I also wanted filmmakers to experience Donegal as more than a location on a screen, but as a place where their work could find an audience and start a conversation. Our masterclasses and workshops in acting, producing and writing are a big part of that. A screening can inspire someone to make a film and practical support can then help them take the first step. I know how much it matters to be able to learn from working people in the industry, ask honest questions and meet others who are trying to find their way in. We are increasingly seeing filmmakers make Disappear Here an established stop in their festival circuit strategy. For many Irish filmmakers, the festival offers a chance to bring their work to a Donegal audience and connect with fellow filmmakers in an intimate setting. Our international engagement is growing too. It is exciting to see films travel to Ballyliffin from further afield, and to watch audiences here respond to stories they might never have encountered otherwise. When Star Wars: The Last Jedi filmed at Malin Head, it brought international attention to Inishowen's coastline. The Northman later used Five Fingers Strand as a filming location. These and a multitude of other productions showed what Donegal could offer a major film crew. Just as encouraging is the growth of filmmaking within the county, the people developing ideas, building skills and creating work of their own.

stories.title: Anna Faris 'hurt' by Chuck Lorre's comments
stories.summary: Mom actress Anna Faris has said she was "hurt" by comments made by showrunner Chuck Lorre and is now sober. Faris, 49, starred in Lorre’s sitcom for seven seasons, from 2013 until 2020. It follows Christy Plunkett, a single mother who restarts her life after dealing with alcohol and substance abuse. Lorre, who was also behind Two and A Half Men and The Big Bang Theory, wrote in his new memoir Sitcom that her unexpected departure validated his initial doubts about casting her in the show. Faris said on Instagram: "Yikes. Yes, I read a few things. I really didn’t see that coming. Of course it hurts. "Chuck gave me a job I loved, and for seven years I never took a day of it for granted. "I’m proud of what we made together, and noting changes how grateful I am for those people and those years.

stories.title: Creative Director McGirr to leave McQueen after 3 years
stories.summary: Seán McGirr, the Dublin-born designer, is exiting storied fashion house McQueen after three years as the brand's Creative Director. Kering, the parent company of the London-based fashion house, made the annoucement today, just weeks after the brand's momentous return to the London Fashion Week circuit. McGirr joined McQueen in 2023, succeeding Sarah Burton, who took over as Creative Director in 2010 after the death of Lee Alexander McQueen and had a career spanning 26 years with the fashion house. That show now feels particularly significant, as McGirr invited jeweller and former McQueen collaborator, Shaun Leane, to create pieces for the runway for the first time in 16 years, fulfilling a long-held ambition of his. McGirr was previously Head of Ready-to-wear at JW Anderson, the eponymous label of Magherafelt native Jonathan Anderson, now the Creative Director of Christian Dior. McGirr originally joined JW Anderson in 2020 to oversee men's collections, before taking on womenswear. McGirr is a graduate of Central Saint Martins where he obtained a Master of Arts in Fashion in 2014 and trained under Louise Wilson, an ambitious professor who mentored and influenced the careers of designers including Christopher Kane, Roksanda Ilincic and Mary Katrantzou.

stories.title: Ukraine's bruising week at the hands of Trump and Putin
stories.summary: In the week when Volodymyr Zelensky had the worst falling out with Donald Trump since the notorious Oval Office ambush 18 months ago, Ukraine’s president is also facing a grave financing problem for next year. Both issues dominated his presence at this week’s EU summit in Brussels. The Oval Office encounter was a straightforward humiliation by the US president and JD Vance; this time around, Donald Trump’s displeasure that Ukraine baulked at stopping attacks on Russian oil refineries had a deadly real-world consequence. The White House both withheld intelligence about imminent Russian ballistic missile attacks and impeded Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite system, meaning that Ukraine’s defence interceptor drones could only fly at 70kmh and were thus no match for Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones which travel at 400kmh. Because Russia has been sending waves of such drones since the summer, the death toll is climbing, with over 150 civilians killed in the past 10 days. While President Zelensky was meeting leaders in Brussels, a Russian drone hit a flea market in Kharkiv, killing two people.

stories.title: Illegal vapes, cannabis-based products worth €3m seized
stories.summary: Gardaí have seized €3 million worth of illegal vapes and cannabis-based products following searches in properties in a number of counties. The searches were carried out on Wednesday in counties Longford, Mayo, Roscommon, Wexford and Carlow as part of an operation targeting organised crime. More than 100 gardaí were involved in the searches and among the items seized were illegal vapes and cannabis-based products with an estimated street value of more than €3m. They are to be sent to Forensic Science Ireland for an analysis. A number of high-value vehicles were also seized, as well as more than €235,000 in cash, £3,000 in sterling and $3,500 in US dollars. Gardaí say that no arrests have been made and investigations are ongoing.

stories.title: Minister 'shocked' at UK decision on Sally Rooney books
stories.summary: Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee has said she was "shocked" that Sally Rooney's books are being removed from UK shops, and will raise the matter with her British counterpart. On Wednesday, Faber confirmed it will stop supplying Rooney's books in the UK, but says copies already held by retailers will not be removed from sale. Ms McEntee has told the Dáil she followed Rooney's work and held it in high regard. Minister McEntee also said she has spoken "a number of times" to her British counterpart, Ed Miliband, "who has set out very clearly" his position in support of Palestine. She said that she "has no problem" raising the matter of Ms Rooney with the UK Foreign Secretary, but cannot comment on another country's laws. She was responding to Social Democrats TD Sinéad Gibney who said that Ms Rooney is one of Ireland's most celebrated authors.

stories.title: HFA posts 26% increase in lending activity in first half
stories.summary: The Housing Finance Agency, which provides financing to support the delivery of social and affordable homes, has reported a 26% increase in lending activity for the first half of this year. The HFA said its funding supported the delivery of 2,611 homes in the first half of 2026. Figures published today show that the agency advanced more than €750m in new lending in the first six months of this year, which supported the delivery of 1,954 social homes and 657 Cost Rental homes. It also said the outlook for further housing delivery remains strong as it approved almost €700m in new funding during the six month period. This will support the planned delivery of a further 2,702 social and affordable homes in the coming years. Publishing its annual report for 2025 today, the HFA said it advanced a total of €2.1 billion in new lending for the year, an increase of 44% on the previous year.

stories.title: Nineteen injured after bus collides with Eurotunnel train
stories.summary: Nineteen people were injured when a minibus collided with a freight train at the loading platform of the Eurotunnel near Calais, French authorities have said. The cause of the accident, which took place in Coquelles last night, has yet to be determined, local authorities added. It appears the minibus, which was transporting heavy goods vehicle drivers, collided with a departing LeShuttle train on the platform, a local official told reporters. The Pas-de-Calais prefecture said in a statement: "An accident involving a minibus carrying heavy goods vehicle drivers, headed to board a LeShuttle train, occurred this evening at the loading platform of the Eurotunnel site. "Significant resources were immediately deployed by Eurotunnel, and subsequently placed under the authority of the Prefect of the Pas-de-Calais department. "Early reports suggest that 19 people were involved, including the driver.

stories.title: Changed Lisowski hopeful season can catch fire in Belfast
stories.summary: A year on from his greatest moment on a snooker table, Jack Lisowski says last year's victory at the Northern Ireland Open changed him as a person. Lisowski had already broken into snooker's exclusive top-16 in the world rankings during the 2018/2019 season, but it was all the more impressive given his failure to land a ranking title. It required a massive level of consistency - four ranking finals, five semi-finals and 14 quarter-finals - in the eight previous seasons, but he had never managed to get over the line. That all changed on the October bank holiday weekend of 2025, when he took the title in Belfast against his good friend Judd Trump. His defence of the title begins tomorrow against Huang Jiahao, but the 35-year-old says he will arrive at the Waterfront Hall as a different person compared to the one that showed up 12 months ago. "It was such a big thing in my life. It was every single interview for like five years, pretty much, or every other interview, they’d say, 'when are you going to win one?'
